explain.say: On 26 July 1956, in Alexandria, Egypt's president Gamal Abdel Nasser told a vast crowd that Egypt was taking over the Suez Canal Company, run mainly by British and French shareholders. When he spoke the name of the canal's builder, de Lesseps, a code word, Egyptian officials seized its offices. Look at the timeline of the crisis that followed.

explain.say: Look at the map. The canal links the Mediterranean to the Red Sea, the short route from Europe to the Gulf and Asia; much of Western Europe's oil passed through it. Nasser said canal fees would pay for the Aswan High Dam after the USA withdrew its funding. Why would one waterway matter so much to London and Paris?

See the motives. Britain's prime minister Anthony Eden saw Nasser as a new Mussolini who must not be appeased. France blamed Nasser for helping Algerian rebels. In October, at Sèvres near Paris, Britain, France and Israel secretly agreed that Israel would attack and the two powers would step in as peacemakers. Why keep that plan secret?

explain.say: Now the network. Israel attacked on 29 October; British and French troops landed at Port Said on 5 and 6 November. But the United States furiously opposed it and put pressure on Britain's currency, the Soviet Union issued threats, while crushing Hungary at the same moment, and the UN demanded a ceasefire. Which link do you think forced Britain to stop?

explain.say: Watch the results. A ceasefire on 6 November, the first large UN peacekeeping force, Eden's resignation in January 1957, and Nasser a hero across the Arab world. Britain learned it could not act against Washington's will. Great work. Exam tip: use Suez to show how power moved from old empires to superpowers.

faq.a: In 1956 Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal Company. Israel, Britain and France then attacked Egypt under a secret plan, but American financial pressure, Soviet threats and UN demands forced a ceasefire and withdrawal. Egypt kept the canal.
asks: Why did Nasser nationalise the canal?

faq.q: Why did Britain and France invade Egypt?
faq.a: They wanted to regain control of the canal, a key oil route, and to topple Nasser. Eden compared him to Mussolini, and France blamed him for supporting Algerian rebels. Israel had its own security aims.
asks: Why did Eden compare Nasser to Mussolini?

faq.q: Why was the Suez Crisis a turning point?
faq.a: It showed that Britain and France could no longer act as great powers against US wishes, boosted Nasser and Arab nationalism, led to the first major UN peacekeeping force and sped up British decolonisation.
asks: What did the USA do during Suez?

faq.q: What was the Protocol of Sèvres?
faq.a: A secret agreement made at Sèvres, near Paris, in October 1956: Israel would invade Sinai, and Britain and France would then issue an ultimatum and occupy the canal zone as supposed peacemakers. Its existence was long denied.
asks: Was the Suez invasion planned in secret?

faq.a: Britain's prime minister from 1955, who ordered the Suez invasion. Humiliated by the forced withdrawal and in poor health, he resigned in January 1957.

facts: Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal Company on 26 July 1956.
A ceasefire came into force at midnight on 6 November 1956.
Lester Pearson won the 1957 Nobel Peace Prize for proposing the UN Emergency Force.
